text: During the Spring and Fall 2024 periods, a ship transecting the study area from north to south (Fig. 1) launched atmospheric soundings at the same times as the land-based soundings as well as collected observations on the cloud and wind conditions via ceilometers and scanning and profiling Doppler lidars. The winter 2024 period conducted coordinated sounding launches from WHOI and from the NOAA ship R/V Pisces, stationed at the location of the barge for ~14 days, as well as additional observations on: aerosols and cloud observations, scanning and profiling Doppler lidar-based winds, and thermodynamic profiles. 15 Table 4. WFIP3 Intensive Operating Period Soundings DATA PRODUCTS AND DATA AVAILABILITY EVENT LOG Throughout the field period, the WFIP3 project team identified and cataloged events of significance for atmospheric research and forecast assessments, including: land-sea breeze events, low-level jets, lulls, fog and precipitation, as well as significant forecast misses. This activity was patterned after a similar effort associated with WFIP2 (Shaw et al. 2019). Weekly analysis of the observed atmospheric state and the quality of the existing NOAA High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR: Dowell et al. 2022) forecast for the period was undertaken by a rotating member of the WFIP3 team with additional support from the local NOAA weather forecasting offices at Upton and Boston. Team members objectively ranked the weather and ocean conditions present for their uniqueness, appearance of short- or small-scale features, and reduced forecast skill. The collective summary of these weekly weather analyses was formulated into an `event log' of weather and ocean events (available at Bodini et al, 2024) that serves as a record of important events for the field campaign and potential case studies for further analysis via observational or modeling studies (Bodini et al. 2025b). Throughout the field period, a number of individual days were determined to be of interest for additional observational assessments due to the presence of small scale phenomena such as low level jets, marine fog, and cold air outbreaks. Case studies of these types of events are detailed below. In general, significant events -- or poor forecast skill -- were more prevalent during the warmer months spanning April to September. UNIFIED WIND AND THERMODYNAMIC PROFILES Unified wind and thermodynamic profiles were developed for each observational site by combining data from multiple sensors into a single estimate of the atmosphere's state, extending from the surface to the top of the boundary layer. Composite wind and atmospheric turbulence profiles relied on a multi- instrument suite of fixed and profiling systems including scanning and profiling lidars, 915-MHz wind 16 profiling radars, and high-frequency sonic anemometers at each land site. All measurements from each sensor were subject to rigorous quality control procedures including: signal-to-noise ratio filtering, tilt and compass error corrections, thresholding of the ensemble averages for minimum data returns, etc. Two separate data products were generated for potential users: The first, WINDPROF (following Newsom and Krishnamurthy 2022; Krishnamurthy et al. 2013), provides standardized 10-minute resolution data, linearly interpolated to a uniform height grid with vertical spacing of 20 m near the surface and 30 m above 100 m
